articles.title: Apple Giving Some Mac Mini Customers a Free Upgrade
articles.subtitle: Apple has informed some customers who recently ordered a Mac mini with an M4 chip that has yet to ship that it will be upgrading their order to an equivalent version of the new Mac mini with an M6 chip at no additional cost.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple has informed some customers who recently ordered a Mac mini with an M4 chip that has yet to ship that it will be upgrading their order to an equivalent version of the new Mac mini with an M6 chip at no additional cost.

Apple's email to customers:

Thank you for your recent Mac order. We know you're looking forward to receiving your purchase. As you may know, Apple recently announced the new Mac mini. Since your order has yet to ship, we automatically upgraded you to the new Mac mini at no additional cost.

Thank you for your recent Mac order. We know you're looking forward to receiving your purchase.

As you may know, Apple recently announced the new Mac mini. Since your order has yet to ship, we automatically upgraded you to the new Mac mini at no additional cost.

Given the Mac mini now starts at $899 instead of $799 in the U.S., some customers are effectively receiving a $100 discount on the new model.

One customer on social media was delighted to learn that they would not only be receiving the new Mac mini at no additional cost, but also saw their delivery estimate bumped up from October to September. On the other hand, a student emailed us to complain that their delivery estimate was pushed back by several weeks as a result of the free upgrade, as they said they need the computer imminently for their studies. The student said Apple did not offer them a choice to accept or decline the free upgrade.

Apple announced the new Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro chip options this week, alongside a new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chip options. Both new Macs are available to pre-order now ahead and launch on Tuesday, September 22.

The previous-generation Mac mini was released in November 2024.

articles.title: New Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra: Everything you need to know
articles.subtitle: Macworld New Mac Studio 2026: At a glance What’s new: The 2026 Mac Studio gains M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, dramatically faster AI and graphics performance, faster SSD storage, increased memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and enhanced professional...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
New Mac Studio 2026: At a glance

What’s new: The 2026 Mac Studio gains M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, dramatically faster AI and graphics performance, faster SSD storage, increased memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and enhanced professional connectivity.

Release date: Announced on August 25, 2026

Price: From $2,499/£2,499

Pre-orders: Pre-order now

On sale: Shipping starts on September 22, 2026 but the Mac Studio with 512GB of unified memory is coming in late October.

Apple has launched a new Mac Studio to replace the M4 Max and M3 Ultra model introduced 17 months ago, in March 2025. Externally, the 2026 Mac Studio retains what Apple calls its “signature compact design,” with the most significant upgrades taking place inside.

The previous generation was unusual because it mixed chip generations, pairing M4 Max with M3 Ultra. The 2026 models bring both tiers into the M5 family, with M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU, while M5 Ultra scales to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Neural Accelerators are now built into every GPU core to boost AI performance.

Apple claims up to 1. 3x faster CPU performance, 1. 8x faster graphics and 4. 3x faster AI performance, depending on the configuration and workload. M5 Max also adds third-generation hardware-accelerated ray tracing, while M5 Ultra can play up to 33 streams of 8K ProRes 422 video simultaneously.

Elsewhere, PCIe Gen 6-based SSDs deliver up to twice the storage performance, while Apple’s N1 chip adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. USB-C genlock, support for up to eight displays, and Thunderbolt 5 clustering for distributed AI workloads are also new.

When is the new Mac Studio available?

The new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra was announced on August 25, 2026, but it won’t start shipping until September 22. Even then, not every configuration will be available: Apple says Mac Studio models configured with 512GB of unified memory won’t arrive until “late October.”

You can pre-order the new Mac Studio now, though, and if you want one we’d recommend ordering early. Ongoing chip and component shortages have constrained Mac availability, so the most popular configurations could quickly become difficult to find.

Pre-order the Mac Studio at Apple

Pre-order the Mac Studio at Apple U.K.

How much does the new Mac Studio cost?

Has the Mac Studio price gone up?

In June 2026, Apple raised the starting price of the Mac Studio by $500, from $1,999 to $2,499. The M3 Ultra model saw an even steeper increase, rising $1,300 from its $3,999 launch price to $5,299. The hikes were part of broader increases across the Mac lineup, which Apple attributed to sharply higher component costs, particularly RAM.

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

articles.title: Apple’s China AI strategy now includes training its own custom model, per report
articles.subtitle: china Apple Intelligence Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
china

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Ubisoft Charges Steam Players $10 For ’90s Classic Heroes Of Might And Magic 3 And Forgets To Actually Give Them The Game
articles.subtitle: Heroes of Might and Magic III RTS Ubisoft The good news is that Ubisoft has brought Heroes of Might and Magic III, a strategy classic from 1999, back to Steam in a content-complete form.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Heroes of Might and Magic III RTS Ubisoft

The good news is that Ubisoft has brought Heroes of Might and Magic III, a strategy classic from 1999, back to Steam in a content-complete form. The bad news is that die-hard fans who rushed to buy it didn’t get the game.

An HD version of the game put on Steam in 2015 lacked the expansions and certain features. “This is the original version of the game from 1999,” reads the new listing on Valve’s storefront. “The pack includes the original Heroes of Might and Magic III and its two expansions: Armageddon’s Blade and The Shadow of Death.”

If you ever feel bad about botching your indie game release, remember that you'll never be as bad as Ubisoft. They literally forgot to upload the actual game. pic.twitter.com/LsPfwyLkvz — Sos "Buy Lazy Kickers" Sosowski (@Sosowski) August 26, 2026

If you ever feel bad about botching your indie game release, remember that you'll never be as bad as Ubisoft.

They literally forgot to upload the actual game. pic.twitter.com/LsPfwyLkvz

— Sos "Buy Lazy Kickers" Sosowski (@Sosowski) August 26, 2026

Unfortunately, when players first went to spend $10 on buying the game and clicked download, they only got a 23.49 KB file that gave them an error message when they tried to launch the game. “Warning DO NOT buy this game, this is frankly so ridiculous they did not even include the game files with this release,” read one angry Steam review.

The person continued, “It only contains a dummy.exe that when you launch the game just loads up CMD, how can you get this wrong?” “Ubisoft you are a well established company and have released so many games on steam, how can you mess up so badly? Avoid this and buy on GOG where it actually works.”

Don’t worry, of course Ubisoft eventually fixed the issue. “Around ~10/~11 hours after the release there was a 770MB update, which finally added game files into the game directory!” announced another player. “Game is working now… I’m still leaving a bad review for that premiere tho. Sorry Heroes 3, it’s not about you, you’re a great game…”

The entire thing is still very funny though, unless you were excited to play Heroes of Might and Magic III last night and ended up getting errors instead. The game’s re-release arrives alongside the announcement that it’s getting a new remake. This overhauled 4K version will bring the game to consoles for the first time, though fans area hopeful it hasn’t ditched the original’s soundtrack by Paul Romero.

articles.title: Apple Magic Keyboards get cosmetic updates, avoid price hikes
articles.subtitle: Macworld If you’re planning on investing in a new M6 Mac mini or M5 Ultra Mac Studio, you might be buying a new Apple Magic Keyboard along with it. Apple has updated its keyboards, too: Certain keys have had their labels changed to symbols instead of names.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
If you’re planning on investing in a new M6 Mac mini or M5 Ultra Mac Studio, you might be buying a new Apple Magic Keyboard along with it. Apple has updated its keyboards, too: Certain keys have had their labels changed to symbols instead of names.

Apple introduced these changes with the MacBook Neo and M5 MacBook Air, so the company is basically catching up on normalizing the keys. The Tab, Caps Lock, Shift, Delete, and Return keys no longer have their respective word labels. Instead, they have arrow icons:

Tab is now ⇥

Caps Lock is now ⇪

Shift is now ⇧

Delete is now ⌫

Return looks similar to ↵ (see photo above)

The switch to the graphical labeling is an effort to standardize its keyboards. Apple’s non-English keyboards have used symbols, and implementing them in the English keyboard streamlines the production process. However, Apple did not update the keys on the $129 wireless Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad that has a Lightning connection for charging.

Speaking of the production process, it appears that the Magic Keyboards have not been affected by the worldwide RAM shortage (/sarcasm), so their prices have not changed:

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

articles.title: 'Star Wars Zero Company' does something the prequels never could
articles.subtitle: Zero Company has a touch more Andor DNA than you’d expect. Let’s make something clear: Despite recent efforts to rehabilitate the Star Wars prequels, these films are simply not very good.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Zero Company has a touch more Andor DNA than you’d expect.

Let’s make something clear: Despite recent efforts to rehabilitate the Star Wars prequels, these films are simply not very good. George Lucas’ final trilogy is defined by flat direction, cumbersome dialogue, and an obsession with 3DCGI tech that makes nearly every scene detached and alienating — a flaw that’s only worsened with time.

Aside from Revenge of the Sith, which still fumbles key moments, these movies are downright tedious, and were rightly panned at release. Even with these flaws, the prequels have one great boon; buried beneath the horrible execution are nuggets of something compelling.

Star Wars Zero Company harvests much of this raw potential. Working in a realm pioneered by the Clone Wars TV series, Bit Reactor and Respawn Entertainment’s turn-based strategy game convincingly places us in the late Republic era, where a band of mercenaries ends up way in over their heads as the world crumbles around them.

Perhaps most impressively, Zero Company does all this within the margins of a tactics game, as you spend dozens of hours methodically blasting Separatists and cult members in cleverly constructed skirmishes. This combination ends up fitting: you spend so much engrossed in what’s right in front of you, as background news briefings and idle chatter point toward something very dark on the horizon. It’s not your problem until it very much is.

You play as Hawks, a disgraced Republic officer in charge of the ailing mercenary crew Zero Company. It’s a ragtag outfit, and while Hawks is former military, their squad takes in all kinds: former Separatists, discharged clones, freedom fighters, legendary warriors, and misfits alike. The group has seen better days.

In an effort to clear their deep debt to the Hutts, Hawks begrudgingly takes a job from a Republic intelligence agent who’s looking into something strange: a spiral-obsessed cult called the Coil. From there, Zero Company gets pulled into a conspiracy that increasingly overlaps with the all-consuming Clone Wars.

Recommended For You

To avoid overemphasizing Zero Company ’s surprisingly compelling storytelling, it’s worth reiterating that most of your time with this very meaty game will be spent fiddling with pieces on a board like you’re playing holochess. At its core, this experience is unabashedly inspired by Firaxis Games’ XCOM: Enemy Unknown. ( Zero Company … ZCOM… Get it?

) You control a small squad, spending action points to move your units across an isometric battlefield. You’ll move these operatives into cover, have them fire shots with a percentage-based chance of success, and even order them to take a defensive position called Overwatch.

In between missions, you’ll prioritize permanent upgrades to your base that improve your units and increase your influence throughout the galaxy, while making decisions about how to improve your troops.

But there’s much more to a sound tactics experience than just checking off XCOM’s boxes, and thankfully, Zero Company understands what makes these games tick: the brain-scratching satisfaction of working through battlefields that fit together like puzzles. As you progress, your crew will unlock increasingly specific abilities associated with their classes, offering the tools needed to solve these combat riddles.

Use a melee bruiser to knock an enemy out of cover, leaving them wide open for your Marksman. Draw aggro with your Heavy, letting your squishier units hit the flanks unharassed. Use the Scoundrel’s powerful Identify Weakness ability to apply Vulnerable, which guarantees a critical hit. Or just cut people in half with a Jedi.

Nearly all of the nine base classes feel fleshed out and useful in some way, especially because you eventually unlock the ability to mix and match. That gives each character a secondary specialization that broadens their toolset and enables sicko synergies. There’s a great deal of freedom to experiment because you can change these classes at any time, tinkering to deal with a particular encounter.

While this seems like it would undermine the game’s general emphasis on tough, permanent choices, there are still lasting consequences to how you build your outfit. As your allies form Bonds with one another, they gain stat buffs that probably benefit some classes over others (your tanklike Heavy wants Health and Defense boosts, and so on).

Add in the fact that many characters have unique abilities that heavily incentivize certain playstyles — the guy with a melee attack that refreshes all his action points after a kill should probably use a melee-focused class — and you’re getting the best of both worlds.

The different enemy types make all the tinkering with weapons, utilities, and skill points worth doing, and while these battles aren’t nearly as harrowing or harsh as in XCOM, the Hard difficulty (which the game recommends for tactics heads) offers enough of a challenge to make it worth thinking through your turns.

There’s a lot to consider, because with careful planning, you can take advantage of buffs, AOE attacks, and moves that let units keep attacking to set up board-clearing plays that are a delight to execute.

articles.title: New Mac Mini Bumps Display Refresh Rates to 165Hz
articles.subtitle: Apple's newly announced M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini models still support up to three external displays, but there's now support for higher refresh rates, according to Apple's published technical specifications.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple's newly announced M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini models still support up to three external displays, but there's now support for higher refresh rates, according to Apple's published technical specifications.

Here's what's changed versus the M4 generation:

The M6 model runs two displays at up to 6K 60Hz or 4K 165Hz, up from 144Hz on M4, plus a third display at up to 5K 60Hz over Thunderbolt or 4K 60Hz over HDMI.

The M5 Pro model runs all three displays at up to 6K 60Hz or 4K 165Hz, up from 144Hz on the M4 Pro.

In a two-monitor setup, the M5 Pro model's second screen now supports 5K 120Hz or 4K 200Hz, whereas the M4 Pro listed 6K 60Hz or 4K 144Hz.

The M5 Pro model supports all three displays through one Thunderbolt port, while the M6 still supports two per port.

Single-display support is unchanged: Both chips support 8K 60Hz, 5K 120Hz, or 4K 240Hz.

As for port compatibility around the back, the M6 model has Thunderbolt 4 supporting DisplayPort 1.4, while the M5 Pro model has Thunderbolt 5 supporting DisplayPort 2.1.

The new models were announced on Tuesday. Pre-orders are open now, with shipping and in-store availability on September 22.

articles.title: Star Wars Zero Company review
articles.subtitle: Getting tactical with the boys.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
What is it Star Wars XCOM, but even better than that sounds. Release date August 27, 2026 Expect to pay $50/£40 Publisher Disney / EA / Respawn / Lucasfilm Developer Bit Reactor Reviewed on Core i5 12600K, RX 9070 XT, 32 GB RAM Multiplayer None Steam Deck Not Likely Link Steam

It's kinda weird that it took somebody this long to make a Star Wars squad tactics game, but studio Bit Reactor has, for all intents and purposes, knocked it outta da park. Star Wars Zero Company is a superbly executed⁠—if familiar⁠—tactics game, but it's also a new all-timer Star Wars story: I'm talking Rogue One, Knights of the Old Republic, TIE Fighter-tier.

Melt away everything else, and it's got a Terminator skeleton of pure XCOM, the trendsetting tactics series many of Bit Reactor's senior developers cut their teeth on. But the studio struck out from there into more uncharted territory: lavish production values, zoomed-in action game-style exploration, and some truly knockout set pieces and story beats.

Crucially, none of it came at the cost of challenge or crunchy complexity. It feels like Bit Reactor has pitched a big tent where tactics sickos, RPG storytelling fans, and Joe Sixpack cinematic console game-enjoyers can truly find something to love, not just tolerate.

Zero to hero

Zero Company takes place in the twilight of the High Republic, and sees you inhabiting a Commander Shepard-y point of view character, Hawks. Hawks is a disgraced former Republic officer and, at least in my save file, a Zabrak (Darth Maul guy) who delivers every line in a charmingly incongruous cowboy drawl.

While Hawks has a largely set character, their gender, appearance, and dress are highly customizable, including your choice of combat class and Bit Reactor's admirable embrace of Star Wars' cantina-going humanoid aliens. I felt a sense of ownership of my Hawks the same way I do with Geralt of Rivia.

The entire cast shares a similar easy charisma, both in your home base crew and recruitable story-centric operators⁠—it's a winning, "family of friends" ensemble straight out of the BioWare playbook. There are a lot of comfortable Star Wars archetypes among them⁠—ponderous-but-loveable alien bruiser, uptight princess, and laconic bounty hunter, to name a few⁠—but, like the comfort zone combat mechanics, they're executed extremely well and belie surprisingly affecting twists.

There is some serious "Aerith dies in Final Fantasy 7" stuff in Zero Company's back half that knocked my socks off, and Bit Reactor went to such great lengths establishing a narrative status quo, the moments that upended it felt like I was getting smacked in the chest.

Even when the story's cruising at a relatively calm clip, your lovable crew can be at each others' throats. The cast has the sense of friction and conflict I'm always looking for in an ensemble, and the ex-Separatist characters are some of my favorites. Former bean counter and Zero Company operations lead Runa is abrasive, smarmy, and unpleasant in the best way, while Umbaran bubble boy Luco hates your guts, as well as those of your clone buddy, Trick.

Zero Company is basically Star Wars A-Team: You're mercs with hearts of gold who do private war stuff for the highest bidder, but in, like, a cool, fun, and ethical way. Galactic Republic Intelligence drops a fat contract in your lap to investigate a kooky cult (it's always a cult), leaving Hawks and crew to turn-based battle their way into saving the galaxy.

You gear up and manage your operation from the Den, a small but well-realized home base in an asteroid-bound smuggler city. From the galaxy map, you can choose to execute from a selection of text-based, noncombat espionage operations reminiscent of the War Table stuff in Dragon Age: Inquisition, while each "Cycle" (read: day) at the Den is capped off with a full-fat combat mission that moves time⁠—and, when appropriate, the story⁠—forward.

You explore the Den with full on, action game-style driving third-person controls, and this is one of Zero Company's neatest tricks. Every environment is as tactile and richly detailed as something in Jedi: Fallen Order, and major story missions even feature exploratory interstitials between the fights. But, as soon as combat starts, Zero Company seamlessly zooms out to a classic, tactical view.

The exploration gameplay is almost painfully simple⁠—interact with points of interest for small bonuses, otherwise you're mostly walking down corridors⁠—but I found it had a really outsized effect in this tactics game context. Even as a first attempt, it adds this revelatory immersive quality, while Bit Reactor managed a level of presentation and wow-factor that I'd love to see in other tactics games and CRPGs.

Squad wipe

You're limited to four squadmates on a mission, and can embark on a variety of odd jobs between main quest blowouts: Hostage rescue, steal the thing, blow the thing up, and the surprisingly rare "kill all the guys." Even on side missions, there's an impish, trolling quality to Zero Company's design that I always love to see.

Enemies will spawn just far enough away that you'll struggle to reach them on a first turn, but they'll have no problem counterattacking after you've committed. Reinforcements often spawn right in your path to an exfiltration, and it seems only enemy snipers have access to the really good rifles that can pinpoint strike you from across the map.

Zero Company's difficulty feels very well-judged to me: I felt pressured enough on Normal, but not overwhelmed. My guys would get downed here and there, but I only had to take a second try on one fight in my playthrough.

The Mac mini boasts fast processors, and rivals even Apple’s most pro computers despite costing significantly less. However, as great as it is, there is a problem with the Mac mini—the at-purchase storage upgrades are pricey and after you buy one, it’s nearly impossible to upgrade its internal components. However, we’re here to help.

There are two basic Mac mini models: the latest M4/M5/M6 mini (5 inches square, 2 inches deep) and older M1/M2 mini (7.7 inches square, 1.4 inches deep). Here, we have rounded up the best hardware upgrades and accessories you can buy for either the old or newer models. Most of the M1/M2 tips work with the Apple Studio, too, as that remains the same size.

Apple doesn’t let you upgrade the Mac mini with inexpensive third-party components such as RAM or internal storage, and it prices its custom-build options at the very high end of affordability. With the earlier Mac mini Apple fixed the RAM to the processor and the SSD to the logic board so they couldn’t be swapped out after you buy one. The M4/M5/M6 mini is different with a detachable SSD but swapping this out is beyond most mere mortals.

Here we look at your best Mac mini upgrade options, adding: storage, memory, screen, speakers and microphone. If you want to jump straight to the reviews:

Hubs and docks for new Mac mini

Hubs and docks for Mac mini M2

Other Mac mini accessories

Upgrading the Mac mini: Adding memory and storage

In our FAQ at the foot of this feature we go into more detail about the difficulties of upgrading the Mac mini’s internal components—as it is with most Macs. There are solutions that are quite messy, such as adding external storage.

Foundry

Adding external storage

The simplest way to add storage to a Mac mini is the same as any other Mac: Connect an external hard drive or SSD using one of the Thunderbolt ports on the back of the computer. Even the slowest Solid-state drives (SSD) are faster than mechanical hard disk drives (HDD), but look out for speed differences—entry-level SSDs provide speeds of around 500MBps, while more advanced models can step up to 2,000MBps or even 6,000MBps. See SSD or HDD in the FAQs.

Another way to add inexpensive portable storage is via an SD or microSD card—once the go-to storage format for camera users but also a great format for cheap and portable backup and archive storage. Sadly, the Mac mini doesn’t have a card reader slot, so you’ll need to add one, such as this UGreen USB-C SD Card Reader for $15.

But these are admittedly ugly methods. You’ll have wires hanging out of the back of your Mac mini and a desk cluttered with drives. It’s neater to keep storage hidden inside. Apple won’t let you do it, but there are some great solutions that we have tested here.

Adding Internal storage

The best option is to get more internal storage in your Mac mini, but Apple’s custom-built pricing means upgrading a 256GB model to 1TB will cost you an extra $500, and 2TB will cost $1,000, while M5 Pro options cost even more: 4TB is $1,800 and 8TB will set you back a whopping $3,800.

If you can’t swing the prices for more storage or just decide later that you need more, there are hardware solutions that connect to the mini without messing up the footprint of the small computer. We’ve tested and reviewed these Mac mini storage accessories for you. The tested Mac mini hubs feature upgradeable and inexpensive internal storage plus a range of extra ports, supporting the NVMe form factors that resemble a stick of chewing gum.

On a day of high-priced product announcements, Apple has offered a crumb of comfort to its more cash-strapped customers: the beloved Polishing Cloth has dropped in price by a whopping 53 percent. Relentlessly memed on for charging a faintly absurd $19 for the square cloth at launch three years ago, the company is now happy to accept just $9 for seemingly the same product.

The common thread uniting Tuesday’s two big Mac updates was prices going up. The M6 Mac mini starts at $899, up from $599 for the equivalent M4 model just two months ago. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, starts at $5,499, a price hike of another $200 over the previous price hike. But the Polishing Cloth went against the grain with a huge price drop.

Apple didn’t send out a press release advertising the nonabrasive fabric accessory’s new bargain price. Instead, it quietly removed the previous store entry (which carried the product code MW693AM/A ) and put up a new one in its place ( MLH74AM/A ) with an updated price. Other than the price and code, it appears to be an identical product with an identical description.

As before, that includes the endlessly amusing Compatibility section, which lists every iPhone and iPad going back to 2012, every single Apple Watch, and a huge list of MacBooks. In some ways, it’s surprising the company bothered to make the list since the description makes it clear that the Polishing Cloth cleans any Apple display, but we appreciate the effort.

Whether this bargain price will last remains to be seen. Unlike other Apple devices the Polishing Cloth is unlikely to be affected by the ongoing memory shortage, but we’ll be monitoring international microfiber shipments with the greatest of interest.

Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The new Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search chats on a Mac, and prepare and send messages.

OpenAI says it is available across all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, with support in both ChatGPT Work and Codex.

That access raises privacy and control questions, so OpenAI stresses that sending remains gated by user approval under the default settings.

Users should take care before granting persistent approval. OpenAI’s plugin guide details the risks and how to revoke access.

It also lists a known issue involving tasks that disable approval prompts: “If your task is set to Full access or otherwise disables approval prompts, Apple Messages may be unable to show the confirmation needed to send. Switch to Ask for approval or Approve for me and try again.”

How OpenAI’s Messages plugin works on the Mac

OpenAI explains that the optional Messages plugin runs locally on the Mac. Like other ChatGPT/Codex features including Computer Use, it relies on macOS system technologies like AppleScript and Accessibility.

The optional Messages plugin is not like the sketchy server-related hacks that try to bring iMessage functionality to Android. It’s simply using files on your Mac with your permission when prompted.

And unlike Siri AI, it doesn’t rely on an index of content from Messages. ChatGPT for Mac only uses the data when directed and with permission.

As you can see below, once enabled by the user, ChatGPT is super clear in what it does with messages, especially sending on your behalf when asked.

For these reasons, it shouldn’t be a privacy concern for Apple. The data exists as files on your Mac, and you need to give ChatGPT permission to work with the files. OpenAI also isn’t the only AI company to develop similar tools. It’s just a benefit of the Mac being a more capable operating system than mobile platforms.

articles.title: AI is 'just a plagiarism machine that makes people lose their jobs' in the eyes of The Talos Principle 3's writers
articles.subtitle: "They're basically incredibly intelligent versions of the autocorrect."
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
How many times do some of the most creative and respected figures in this industry need to explain not only why AI is not the key to making a good game, but that it's actually detrimental to creativity? Or as Dispatch's creative director cleanly put: "maybe it's a creative solution if you aren't creative".

We've seen Larian's lead writer trash talk it, saying that AI-generated text is "a 3/10 at best". PUBG founder Brendan Greene has explained how "it's like a race to the middle of shit" as AI content becomes less and less trustworthy. When asked how Take-Two uses AI to help make successful games its CEO, Zelnick, simply said "clones don't sell". Hell, even the king of overpromising Peter Molyneux is tepid when it comes to using it.

But here we are, beating the same damn horse that just won't die as The Talos Principle 3's writers explain why they're also cautious about AI, the lies it tries to sell, and its actual impact on this industry.

"I'm going to talk for myself," Jonas Kyratzes, narrative designer, says in an interview with Game Informer. "I think it's largely ludicrous. I think the technology itself is very impressive, and I think machine learning has tremendous applications, most of which we're currently not seeing or getting.

"I think, because in a profit-oriented system, a lot of the things that we needed to do, we're just not going to use it for, because we're going to use it for stupid things instead, for people to try and make vast amounts of money before their companies collapse."

Kyratzes notes that it's not a clear-cut situation, though, as the technology itself "has a number of very interesting applications" which are unfortunately overshadowed by "these excessive quasi-religious claims" which are "not rooted in any kind of reality." Such as DeepMind's CEO claiming that humanity will experience widespread change that's "10 times bigger than the Industrial Revolution" or Altman saying the AI singularity is already upon us.

"I think a lot of them are also mainly just meant to juice up the stock market," Kyratzes adds. "It's so complicated because the current AI conversation is kind of a bit strange in that some of the time we're talking about something that we call AI, but it's not artificial general intelligence. It's LLMs or machine learning in various forms, which aren't necessarily the same as artificial intelligence in the sense of conscious being."

Kyratzes is right: We've gotten into the unhealthy habit of referring to everything that sits under the 'AI umbrella' as AI, when in a lot of cases, the actual technology is either vastly different than what we're describing it to be, has already been alive and kicking in the industry for years now, or is simply not as ground-breaking as some would have you believe.

"I'm with Jonas in that the LLMs that we're currently dealing with, they're basically incredibly intelligent versions of the autocorrect that I have on my phone," narrative designer Verena Kyratzes says. "And calling them actual AI, general AI, is just ludicrous. I think in the current system that we have, it's just a plagiarism machine that makes people lose their jobs. But I want to have hope that it's a good thing. It's very troublesome to me."

But even still AI isn't a total write-off for Kyratzes, especially since AI isn't even the sole catalyst for some of the most pressing issues which have risen around it. "I'm not against any technology in and of itself," he adds. "So, to me, a lot of the questions are not questions of the technology.

"For example, when a lot of jobs are being lost because of AI, I don't think that that's an AI issue. I think that's a labour issue. That is, why is the power of labour relative to capital so weak? So low that we can't defend ourselves against the owners just eliminating everyone? Like, what's happened to, you know, militant labor, for example. Where is that?"

articles.title: M5 vs. M6 Chip Buyer's Guide: How Much Better Really Is M6?
articles.subtitle: Apple yesterday announced the M6, its first chip built using a 2nm process and the first Apple silicon design to use three different CPU core types, but how does it compare to the M5?
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple yesterday announced the M6, its first chip built using a 2nm process and the first Apple silicon design to use three different CPU core types, but how does it compare to the M5?

Compared to the M5 chip that Apple launched in October 2025, the M6 delivers:

Up to 1.2x faster multithreaded CPU performance.

Nearly 30% higher peak GPU compute for AI.

Up to 2x peak Neural Engine compute.

50% higher geometry rates for complex graphics.

10% higher unified memory bandwidth.

Apple did not publish real-world benchmarks comparing the M6 to the M5 directly, instead framing its Mac mini figures against the M4 and M1 models:

Up to 13.5x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio versus ‌M1‌, and up to 4.8x faster versus the M4.

Up to 2.3x faster spreadsheet calculations in Microsoft Excel versus ‌M1‌, and up to 1.5x faster versus the M4.

Up to 2x faster gaming performance with ray tracing in "Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition" versus the M4.

The most significant architectural change is in the CPU. The M5 splits its ten cores into performance and efficiency groups, which is an arrangement Apple silicon has used since the ‌M1‌. The M6 adds a third tier called "super cores," which handle single-threaded workloads and which Apple says give the chip the world's fastest single-threaded performance.

The performance cores join them for heavier multithreaded work, while the efficiency cores take background tasks. The second major change is the Neural Engine, which is now doubled, with system frameworks able to use both engines at once so apps see faster model execution without any work from developers required. Other hardware changes compared to the M5 include:

The move to a 2nm process is a significant technical change. Apple chips have used FinFET transistors for years, but the M6's N2 process uses a newer design with gate-all-around nanosheet transistors. This means that the transistor's gate wraps around the channel on every side, giving it better control and reducing power leakage at tiny sizes.

TSMC says N2 can offer 10–15% more speed at the same power, or 25–30% lower power use at the same speed, compared with its N3E process. But the M5 uses the newer N3P process, not N3E, so the actual M5-to-M6 improvement is likely to be smaller than those figures suggest.

The M6 is a broad but fairly modest upgrade. It improves the CPU, GPU, Neural Engine, and memory bandwidth, rather than delivering a dramatic gain in one area. The M5's biggest leap was in AI-focused GPU performance, thanks to Neural Accelerators built into each GPU core. The M6's reported 1.2× multithreaded CPU gain and 10% increase in memory bandwidth are good refinements rather than step-changes.

Single-threaded performance is the main exception. Some tasks cannot be split across many CPU cores, including code compilation, file indexing, image editing, and parts of agentic AI workflows. These tasks depend heavily on the speed of one core, and the M6's new "super cores" are designed to improve that directly. A doubled Neural Engine should also help with local AI models, while the larger GPU can process prompts faster.

For everyday work and general responsiveness, the difference will probably be difficult to notice. The M5 already has more than enough performance for normal use, so there is little general-purpose reason to upgrade from an M5 to an M6.

articles.title: Apple announces the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with up to 512GB of RAM
articles.subtitle: Macworld While all eyes are on the upcoming iPhone event, Apple threw us a curveball Tuesday morning with a rare August launch of an updated Mac Studio with the all-new M5 Ultra processor.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
While all eyes are on the upcoming iPhone event, Apple threw us a curveball Tuesday morning with a rare August launch of an updated Mac Studio with the all-new M5 Ultra processor.

The new Mac Studio is visually identical to the previous model but has major upgrades inside. Instead of the M4 Max and M3 Ultra, you can now buy a Mac Studio with an M5 Max or M5 Ultra processor, with up to a whopping 512GB of RAM. Here are the specs Apple is offering for the two chips:

While the M5 Ultra is still double the capability of the M5 Max, Apple touts its “next-generation UltraFusion technology to form a quad-die architecture for the first time in an M-series chip.” The previous UltraFusion interconnector linked two Max dies over 10,000 high-speed connections that offer low latency and high bandwidth. It was previously reported that Apple was working to create a new version of the Ultra chip with more advanced UltraFusion architecture.

Apple is leaning hard into AI and calls the M5 Ultra Mac Studio “a game changer for AI workloads” and says “AI coding agents process significantly faster, image generation tools can render creations in an instant, and enterprise teams can cluster multiple systems to scale performance to new heights.”

In addition to the new chips, the Mac Studio now has an N1 chip to bring Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, as well as “a next-generation SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6.” We already praised the MacBook Pro for its super-fast storage speeds, and Apple now claims the new SSDs deliver “industry-leading read and write speeds for rapid project loading, file transfers, and loading huge LLMs.”

Now for the not-so-good news. While the M5 Max model starts at the same $2,499 as the post-price-hike M4 Max, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio now starts at $5,499, an increase of another $200 over the previous price hike. That means you’re paying $1,500 more than if you bought an M3 Ultra Mac Studio before June.

You’re also paying more for storage and RAM, so get ready to shell out well over 20 grand for a fully loaded model (which won’t be available until October). The most expensive M5 Ultra you can get now, with 256GB of RAM and 16TB of storage, costs $18,299.

The M5 Mac Studio is available for pre-order now but won’t begin shipping until September 22.

articles.title: Meta AI is now available as a more capable desktop app for Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI. Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI.

Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.

Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app.

Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Beyond chat, the sidebar includes Media, Artifacts, scheduled tasks, conversation history, and an “About Me” personalization section.

Users can switch among thinking modes, attach files, generate media, and create recurring briefings or reminders. The app also includes the ability to hide the Dock icon, allowing it to be invoked with a keyboard shortcut instead.

Meta’s recent AI push

The Mac app is the latest in a steady run of releases. In April, Meta replaced Llama with Muse Spark. A May update then expanded Meta AI with more natural voice conversations and live camera-based assistance.

July brought Muse-powered image generation to Meta AI, WhatsApp, and Instagram, although Meta quickly removed one feature that generated images from public Instagram posts. Meta AI also moved into Threads DMs for private chats.

Most recently, Meta launched Muse Code, a terminal-based AI coding agent for macOS and Linux.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Rockstar responds to GTA 6 leaks: 'This is not how we intended for you see the game after all this time'
articles.subtitle: The studio has described the leaks as "heartbreaking for our team".
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
The news cycle this past week has been dominated with Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks, and for good reason, Rockstar studios has sprung a big one, with the self-ordained "Cyberleek" drumming up attention with waves of public manifestos, statements, and a little crypto farming on the side.

In preparation for its somewhat-confusing Netflix-exclusive gameplay reveal tomorrow, Rockstar's finally acknowledged the leaks. Both confirming that they're real beyond a shadow of a doubt (not that there was much doubt to begin with), and trying to salvage some hype.

"We know that many of you have been waiting to hear from us regarding the events of the past week," reads a post to Rockstar's Instagram. "It would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto 6 gameplay leak in this way has been heartbreaking for our team, and this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time.

"We are very sorry that everything has taken as long as it has—from getting the game finished (nearly there!) to sharing more details and official gameplay, and providing the community with everything you want to know."

I'm not sure Rockstar needs to apologise for a videogame taking a long time to make, especially when 13 years have already passed since the last, but I'm a little old-fashioned in that I don't think players are owed much of anything beyond fair consumer practices and, like, maybe getting to actually own the things they buy.

It is, however, intriguing that the studio's apologising for that given the whole Netflix thing which, speaking cynically, is essentially a six-hour early access gated behind a streaming service subscription.

I do feel bad for the developers, though—especially given that even those who were unceremoniously fired (in such a dramatic fashion that the then-UK Prime Minister commented on it ) still want people to see the fruits of their labour. Take-Two's bottom line has likely barely been dented by the leaks, but if I were a person working on a videogame for years, I'd be pretty exhausted by someone making a circus out of it.

"We are very excited for everyone to see the extended look tomorrow. It has taken longer than we wanted to get it ready, but as with everything we do, we know we need to exceed your expectations, and we are determined to deliver at the level you expect and deserve. While it is unfortunate that the intended game experience may now be impacted by some spoilers, we hope that everyone will wait a bit longer to experience the game for themselves on November 19."

Rockstar ends the letter with a show of thanks: "We want to thank everyone in the community who has reached out with messages of support this past week—your words have meant more to this team than you can imagine. Ultimately, we are making this game for you, and without you, we would not have the privilege of making games."

articles.title: Mac-ify your iPad with these 10 must-have accessories
articles.subtitle: Macworld Every year, iPadOS borrows a couple of desktop features, bringing Apple’s tablet closer to the Mac. At this point, some professionals have effectively replaced their MacBooks with iPads, simplifying their setups and making them more portable.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
Every year, iPadOS borrows a couple of desktop features, bringing Apple’s tablet closer to the Mac. At this point, some professionals have effectively replaced their MacBooks with iPads, simplifying their setups and making them more portable. An iPad on its own, however, is insufficient to mimic a MacBook.

One cannot practically type long-form text using the virtual keyboard or rely exclusively on touch controls for daily tasks. Fortunately, with just a few accessories, you can completely transform your iPad experience and upgrade it to a MacBook-like computer.

Keyboard

A keyboard is the most essential productivity accessory you can get for your iPad. Not only does it make typing more intuitive, but it also unlocks advanced keyboard shortcuts across apps—accelerating your workflows in the process. Luckily, iPadOS supports a wide range of keyboards, including most standard Bluetooth ones.

Apple sells the Magic Keyboard for various iPad models, which doubles as a stand and protective case. It also includes an embedded trackpad, essentially turning your iPad into a laptop. For something more budget-friendly, you can’t go wrong with the Logitech Keys-to-Go Bluetooth Keyboard. It is designed specifically for Apple products, supports multi-device connections, and features a portable design.

Foundry

Mouse

Like keyboards, iPadOS supports most Bluetooth mice and trackpads, and will show a dedicated cursor when using one. This spares you from touching the display for interacting with on-screen elements and replicates the Mac experience. For a reliable, ergonomic mouse, go with the Logitech MX Master 4. It features a comfortable build and long battery life, making it suitable for long work hours.

If you’d rather spend less, you can buy a Microsoft-branded Bluetooth mouse for a fraction of the price. It may not offer as many customization options or perks as certain alternatives, but it’ll reliably get the job done.

External display

iPadOS is natively compatible with external monitors, letting you get work done on larger displays. M-series iPads support secondary workspaces, allowing you to simultaneously interact with different windows on the built-in screen and external one. Less powerful iPad models limit external display support to screen mirroring, which is still decent for those seeking a wider canvas.

For a dependable option, you may want to consider the Dell 27 Monitor S2725QC. It features a 4K resolution, USB-C connectivity, 120Hz refresh rate, and more. Planning to work on the go? Go with the Asus ZenScreen 15. 6 Inch Portable Monitor instead. It may not be as advanced, but it’s certainly sufficient for mobile setups.

Foundry

USB-C dongle

iPads only offer a single USB-C port, and that can limit the peripherals you can connect to them—especially during charging sessions. Fortunately, you can add more ports to your iPad by connecting a dongle. There are endless options offered by a wide range of brands, featuring various port types and price ranges that cater to all sorts of customers. Some solid dongles include those from Anker, Acer, and Ugreen. Ensure your iPad model is compatible with your selection before completing your purchase.

Docking Station

If you’re not a big fan of dangling dongles, you could opt for a docking station instead. Several excellent brands offer dedicated stands that incorporate additional ports for your iPad. They are ideal for stable setups and will maintain your desk’s minimalistic, clutter-free look. The Satechi 6-in-1 USB-C Stand Hub and Anker 551 USB-C Hub with Foldable Stand will both transform your iPad into a serious workstation.

articles.title: Apple launches new M6 Mac mini with another price hike
articles.subtitle: Macworld As predicted on this site earlier today, Apple has announced the launch of a new Mac mini model with M5 and M6 chip options.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
As predicted on this site earlier today, Apple has announced the launch of a new Mac mini model with M5 and M6 chip options. It doesn’t feature any design changes or external upgrades, but it does offer a two-generation bump in processors compared to the previous model.

Slightly confusingly, the version of the Mac mini with a chip from the M5 generation is the more powerful of the two, because it’s the M5 Pro. This spec starts at $1,699 for a 15-core CPU and 16-core GPU, but customers have the option to bump that to 18 and 20 cores, respectively, for an additional $200.

There are also configuration options to increase RAM from the starting 24GB or storage from the baseline 512GB, and to upgrade to 10 Gigabit Ethernet. The RAM options remain the same, but the 64GB highest-end option now costs $1,000.

More appealing for the Mac mini’s traditional budget market will be the M6 model, which starts at a far more manageable $899. That, however, is still a $100 increase over the M4 model from 2024 that it replaces. Worse, the M4 model started at just $599 until June, when Apple responded to the ongoing memory crunch by imposing brutal price hikes. In other words, the cheapest entry point to Apple’s desktop Mac ecosystem has jumped by $300, or 50 percent, in the space of two months.

The $899 version isn’t exactly a state-of-the-art build, either. The entry-level configuration comes with 16GB of RAM and just 256GB of storage. We should note that it is possible to get this spec for $799, but only if you’re an education buyer. Of note, the Mac mini is not available for the Apple Upgrade program either.

Apple

The price hike is likely to weaken the Mac mini’s appeal among budget buyers, but (aside from the necessity to accommodate increasing component costs) Apple may not care. In his report predicting that a new mini was on the way, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman noted that the machine had become increasingly popular for running AI applications locally, and that Apple was struggling to meet demand.

The company may not mind if fewer customers are prepared to pay the asking price, since there are plenty of AI fans ready to take their place.

Those AI fans will likely be tempted by a new model with a new chip. Apple boasts that the M6 delivers “gains across every dimension of performance” and “the ideal balance of performance, power efficiency, and on-device AI to effortlessly fly through daily tasks, coding, and creative projects.”

In numerical terms, the company claims the M6 version of the Mac will deliver up to 4x faster AI performance, 2x faster storage and graphics, and 40% faster CPU performance than the M4 mini. The M5 Pro model, meanwhile, is rated by its maker as up to 8.5x faster at LLM prompt processing than its M2 Pro predecessor, and up to 4x faster than the M4 Pro model. Naturally we will put those claims to the test in our labs.

Another surprise is how early Apple has announced the new Mac mini. Pre-orders are open now, but it won’t go on sale until 22 September, almost a month from now.

articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Apple showcases its new developer AI tools in impressive 90-minute presentation
articles.subtitle: Apple today shared a 90-minute WWDC26 presentation recorded live at a packed Steve Jobs Theater, featuring impressive demos of its latest AI tools for developers and an entire app built from just a few prompts.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple today shared a 90-minute WWDC26 presentation recorded live at a packed Steve Jobs Theater, featuring impressive demos of its latest AI tools for developers and an entire app built from just a few prompts. Watch it below

Live session held at the Steve Jobs Theater during WWDC26 now available

The Apple Developer YouTube channel shared an interesting 90-minute WWDC26 session today called “ Inside Apple Intelligence and Xcode: Special Presentation. ”

While parts of the presentation can get technical, after all, this is a WWDC session, the video offers very interesting insight into what developers will be able to build using the new technologies, frameworks, and APIs it announced during the event.

Perhaps one of the more interesting parts of the video is a 20-minute segment in which an entire app is built from a single prompt and then further tweaked with follow-up commands.

articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
They're "very sorry everything has taken as long as it has"

Rockstar Games have put out a statement publicly acknowledging the ongoing GTA 6 leaks for the first time. Though they and parent company Take-Two have already gotten the ball rolling on hunting down the leaker, the studio had stayed silent in terms of public-facing comms up until now.

"We know that many of you have been waiting to hear from us regarding the events of the past week," the statement posted to Rockstar's socials starts. "It would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay leak this way has been heartbreaking for our team, and this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time.

"We are very sorry that everything has taken as long as it has — from getting the game finished (nearly there! ) to sharing more details and official gameplay, and providing the community with everything you want to know," it continues. "We are very excited for everyone to see the Extended Look tomorrow.

It has taken longer than we wanted to get it ready, but as with everything we do, we know we need to exceed your expectations, and we are determined to deliver at the level you expect and deserve. While it is unfortunate that the intended game experience may now be impacted by some spoilers, we hope that everyone will wait a bit longer to experience the game for themselves on November 19th. "

pic.twitter.com/KGqoxFqYho — Rockstar Games (@RockstarGames) August 26, 2026

pic.twitter.com/KGqoxFqYho

So, the studio have made peace with the fact they might not be able to stop the leakers from sharing bits of the game's story. Another bit of the statement which sticks out to me is the part apologising for it having taken so long for Rockstar to share details about and gameplay from GTA 6 via official channels.

It's certainly not excusing the leaks, but does read like an acknowledgement that the fact the studio have waited so long to show the game in action has contributed to the growing appetite players have to see that as release creeps ever closer, a fix many will have settled for getting by dissecting every one of the leaked clips.

"We want to thank everyone in the community who has reached out with messages of support this past week — your words have meant more to this team than you can imagine," Rockstar said in closing. "Ultimately, we are making this game for you, and without you, we would not have had the privilege of making games."

As mentioned in the statement, an "extended look" at GTA 6 is set to premiere on Netflix tomorrow, August 27th. It'll hit YouTube six hours after that Netflix debut.
